title: Git
html:
Git

A content-addressed store of snapshots, plus pointers into it. Almost every confusing behaviour makes sense once that is the model in your head, rather than "a series of diffs".

The model

A commit is a snapshot of the whole tree plus parent pointers and metadata; its identity is a hash of its content, which is why history cannot be edited in place - rewriting produces different commits. A branch is a movable pointer to a commit. HEAD points at your current branch.

Diffs are computed on demand between snapshots, not stored.

The three areas

Working directory, staging area (index), repository. add moves changes to staging, commit moves staging to the repository. The staging area exists so you can commit a subset of what you changed - the reason to keep it rather than commit everything at once.

Merge or rebase

Merge creates a commit with two parents. History is truthful and non-linear.

Rebase replays your commits onto a new base, producing new commits with new hashes. History is linear and easier to read, and it is a rewrite.

The rule that avoids most pain: never rebase anything other people have pulled. Rewriting shared history forces everyone else to reconcile a history that no longer exists. Rebase your own unpushed work freely.

merge --squash collapses a branch to one commit - useful when the intermediate commits are noise rather than history.

Undoing, by what you want

Want Command Rewrites history
Unstage, keep changes reset (mixed) no
Discard local changes restore / checkout -- no
Undo a pushed commit safely revert no - adds an inverse commit
Move the branch pointer back reset --hard yes - destructive
Set aside work temporarily stash no

revert is the safe one for shared branches because it adds rather than removes. reset --hard discards work with no confirmation; check status first, every time.

Finding things

log with --oneline --graph to see shape. blame for who last touched a line, and why - the commit message is the point, not the name. bisect to find the commit that introduced a defect by binary search over history, which is dramatically faster than reading diffs. reflog records where HEAD has been, and recovers commits you thought you destroyed - most "I lost my work" situations end there.

Working with others

Small commits with messages that say why; the diff already says what. A branch per unit of work, reviewed before merging. Pull before pushing. Never commit secrets - and if you do, rotate them, because rewriting history does not un-publish what was fetched.

.gitignore for build output and local settings. Committed build output is how repositories become enormous and how merge conflicts become pointless.

Common mistakes

  • Rebasing a shared branch.
  • reset --hard on the wrong commit, losing uncommitted work.
  • Committing generated files, dependencies or secrets.
  • One enormous commit at the end of a day, so nothing can be reverted or reviewed independently.
  • Resolving a conflict by taking one side wholesale without reading both.
